claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary FCC alloys are primarily caused by differences in local chemical short-range order.
Differences in local chemical short-range order produce different degrees of lattice distortion.
Differences in local chemical short-range order modify stacking-fault-energy distributions.
The resulting lattice-distortion and stacking-fault-energy differences govern dislocation mobility during deformation.
The compared thermomechanically processed quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC with comparable grain sizes and phase homogeneity.
Higher chemical complexity in the quinary alloy promotes more pronounced short-range order than in its quaternary and ternary subsets.
More pronounced short-range order increases local lattice distortion.
Greater local lattice distortion raises energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Reduced component diversity in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces less pronounced short-range order.
Less pronounced short-range order in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces lower lattice distortion.
Lower lattice distortion permits easier dislocation glide in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Differences in dislocation mobility affect yield strength.
Differences in dislocation mobility affect strain hardening.
Under identical deformation conditions, the quinary alloy will have higher yield strength than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Under identical deformation conditions, the quinary alloy will have a steeper strain-hardening rate than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Microscopy or atom-probe measurements will reveal more significant local ordering in the quinary alloy.
Microscopy or atom-probe measurements will reveal greater local lattice distortion in the quinary alloy.
At room temperature and the selected fixed strain rate, dislocation slip and twinning remain active and comparable across the samples.
